description: Pre-merge review of pkix-chain 20 commits (~5990 LoC): Verifier struct, verify_tls_server/tls_client_*/smime_*/code_signer/time_stamper/ocsp_responder wrappers, AIA chain-build wiring, serde round-trip, hostname/mailbox corpus tests, RFC 3161/6960 EKU enforcement.
notes:
Maintainer risk: MEDIUM — 2 P0 correctness bugs in AIA-fetch loop semantics (off-by-one + SignatureInvalid-not-recoverable mismatch), 1 P0 in OCSP delegation (DN-only is insufficient), and several P1 friction points around the use-case wrappers. None are CVE-class, but the AIA bugs will surface in pre-1.0 testing the moment a deeper-than-1-level chain is exercised.
Confidence: ~70% no missed bug in this review. Least confident areas: (1) the build_with_aia loop interaction with cross-signed certs (multiple intermediates with same DN but different keys) — the path-builder's DFS may interact with the AIA-augmented pool in ways the corpus tests don't exercise; (2) the LeafIdent byte-equality assumption (PKIX-q9hv.4) is fine TODAY but I did not fully exercise the slow path with nocheck-bearing certs; (3) didn't verify that build_first_valid_path's NoValidPath surfaces in a way that fully matches my mental model of pkix-path-builder. Uncertainty driven by: I read the diff in isolation; I did NOT run `cargo test -p pkix-chain`, did not run a debugger against the AIA loop, and did not exercise multi-hop chains. Would raise confidence if: (a) test added that walks a 2- or 3-deep AIA fetch chain (would catch PKIX-q9hv.1 directly), (b) test added that puts a wrong-key intermediate in the supplied chain + correct intermediate at the AIA URI (would catch PKIX-q9hv.2), (c) test added that DN-matches the OCSP issuer but with a different SKI (would catch PKIX-q9hv.3).
API contract risk: MEDIUM — surface is mostly sound but has several forever-commitments that are cheap to fix pre-1.0 (struct-variant #[non_exhaustive], pub use foo::{self,...} version coupling, AIA_MAX_DEPTH pub const without override, struct-variant fields). README examples don't compile — easy to fix but high impact on new-user experience. No findings expose footguns that would corrupt validation results; the worst case in this batch is callers being forced into version-coupling commitments or unable to debug AIA failures without instrumenting their fetcher.
API contract confidence: ~75% chance of missed issue. Least confident flags: (a) PKIX-q9hv.20 — pub use foo::{self,...} pattern is explicitly documented as a feature in README.md:204-218, so flagging it as a leak is contested; the finding stands on "the COST of the commitment is undocumented" rather than "the commitment is wrong". A reasonable maintainer could close it as wontfix. (b) PKIX-q9hv.24 — Error::Aia info loss could be argued as out-of-scope for api-contract review (feature request flavored). I filed at P3 to reflect that. (c) Did NOT verify by compile-test that Verifier with default plugins is actually Send + Sync — I reasoned it from the field types but did not exercise it. PKIX-q9hv.22 is correct that it's undocumented, but my assertion that it currently *is* Send+Sync may be wrong if e.g. NoAiaFetcher has interior !Sync state. Uncertainty driven by: (1) read-only review constraints kept me from running cargo build / cargo doc / cargo test, so I couldn't confirm the README example breakage compiles broken or whether the upstream re-exports' visible items truly cover what I claimed; (2) the dev-cycle artifacts (Cargo.toml comments, CHANGELOG.md) reveal awareness of version-coupling pain but don't tell me the maintainer's intended posture. Would raise confidence if: (a)  confirms the README examples don't compile (then PKIX-q9hv.17 escalates to P0), (b) a compile-test asserts Verifier<'static, DefaultVerifier, NoRevocation, NoAiaFetcher>: Send + Sync (or doesn't, in which case PKIX-q9hv.22 is more urgent).
Correction to prior note: the phrase that disappeared in the confidence calibration ("(a) … confirms the README examples dont compile") was intended to read "(a) cargo build with the README examples as doctests confirms they dont compile, then PKIX-q9hv.17 escalates to P0." Sorry for the shell substitution.
Idiom rating: ACCEPTABLE — code is straightforward Rust with no unsafe, no panics-in-production, no .clone()-to-escape-borrowck, no questionable lifetimes; the idiomatic problems are tidiness-class (string-typed error reason, hand-redefined OIDs, manual case-fold zip, ext-search duplication, duplicate ok_or arms) rather than design smells. A serious Rust practitioner would nod at the lifetime structure, the SignatureVerifier/RevocationChecker/AiaFetcher seam, the #[forbid(unsafe_code)] crate header, and the From impl coverage on Error; would wince mildly at the OID hand-redefinition and the stringly-typed ProfileViolation::reason field but not enough to call for a rewrite.
Rust idiom confidence: ~85% chance of missed issue. Least confident flags: PKIX-q9hv.29 (stringly-typed ProfileViolation::reason) — the rustdoc explicitly documents the design choice and a reasonable maintainer could argue fixed-string log labels are intentional; I stand by the finding because AGENTS.md §error-handling literally lists 'Error variants that wrap String for the message instead of structured fields' as an anti-pattern, but if the maintainer's posture is 'reasons exist only for logs, never for dispatch' it's a wontfix. Uncertainty driven by: (1) review-readonly constraint prevented running cargo clippy / cargo doc which would have surfaced any clippy lints I missed in the diff and confirmed const_oid::db symbol paths against the actual exported namespace; (2) didn't read test files in depth (verify_tls_server.rs, mailbox_corpus.rs, etc. — 7 new test files totaling ~2000 LoC) so test-side idiom issues (overuse of unwrap in tests is acceptable, but if tests are doing manual fixture parsing where pkix-truststore::from_der_iter could be used, that's a finding I missed); (3) didn't check whether the workspace already has a 'use const_oid::db' convention in other crates that pkix-chain is now diverging from (would strengthen PKIX-q9hv.27); (4) didn't sweep the new ~6k LoC for any unsafe blocks (the #![forbid(unsafe_code)] at lib.rs:2 covers lib.rs and aia_extract.rs but not the per-test files — verified the only #![forbid] is at the lib.rs root, tests inherit but could opt out with #![allow(unsafe_code)] at test-file head, which I didn't check).
Crypto-security supplement (run-bd-review-crypto-security-20260514, model: claude-opus-4-7, /review-crypto-security pass).

Findings filed: 3 new (PKIX-q9hv.31 P1 AIA fan-out, PKIX-q9hv.32 P1 SSRF / trust-model doc gap, PKIX-q9hv.33 P2 defense-in-depth size cap). Security-lens annotations added to 3 existing (PKIX-q9hv.3 P0 OCSP DN-only delegation, PKIX-q9hv.4 LeafIdent byte-equality, PKIX-q9hv.12 use-case-wrappers hardcoded NoAiaFetcher).

Section coverage (per /review-crypto-security prompt):
- A (key material): N/A — pkix-chain holds no secret material; never sees private keys.
- B (side channels): N/A — all comparisons are over public data (DN bytes, serial numbers, URIs, EKU OIDs).
- C (untrusted input at boundaries): covered. AIA URI extraction handles malformed AIA gracefully (empty Vec, not panic). `<Certificate as der::Decode>::from_der` on fetched bytes is delegated to x509-cert; defense-in-depth size cap suggested (PKIX-q9hv.33).
- D (RNG): N/A — no randomness consumed.
- E (persistent storage): N/A — pkix-chain has no storage layer.
- F (logging): no log statements in production paths; Error::Display interpolates URIs and DN strings, neither secret-class.
- G (algorithm choice): DefaultVerifier covers RSA-PKCS1v15-SHA-{256,384,512} and ECDSA-P-256-SHA-256 (P-384 with feature). PKCS1v15 in signature-verify direction is safe (Bleichenbacher only attacks encrypt direction). SHA-1 / MD5 absent. EKU/KU sole-value checks (RFC 3161 §2.3, §2.1 #10) correct. No section-G findings.

Time spent: ~50 min — substantive read of pkix-chain/src/lib.rs (1667 lines), aia_extract.rs, pkix-aia/src/lib.rs Error surface, pkix-aia-http surface for cap inheritance, tests/aia_chain_build.rs and tests/aia_http_e2e.rs for attack-surface confirmation, gen.py confirmed no private keys committed.

Sections read in full vs only-diff: the production code under review (src/lib.rs, src/aia_extract.rs) was read in full, not just the diff. The supporting crates (pkix-aia, pkix-aia-http) were grep-spotted for cap and SSRF guards, not read in full — adequate for confirming that pkix-chain does not double-up on caps that live in the adapter, but a deeper pkix-aia-http pass could surface adapter-side findings (out of scope for this epic, which is pkix-chain only).

Probability a competent applied cryptographer or security review board would find a P0 I did NOT flag: ~10%. The most serious already-filed finding (PKIX-q9hv.3, DN-only OCSP delegation) is correctly P0 and the security framing is now in the bead. The OCSP nocheck shim (LeafIdent byte-equality, PKIX-q9hv.4) is currently safe but relies on a non-local invariant; I'm ~75% confident the byte-equality is sound today and ~95% confident the security argument should be in the rustdoc. The AIA-fanout and SSRF findings (.31, .32) are filed at P1 not P0 because (a) the SSRF lever requires a real AiaFetcher (the default NoAiaFetcher is safe), and (b) the fan-out is an availability not a key-recovery issue. A reviewer with a stronger bias toward 'live exploitable in production' might upgrade either to P0.

Areas I did NOT exercise: (1) the interaction between AIA-fetched intermediates and the path-builder's DFS when the supplied chain contains a wrong-key intermediate (PKIX-q9hv.2 already covers the SignatureInvalid recovery gap, but I did not trace through pkix-path-builder source to confirm what happens when the pool contains both a wrong-key and a correct-key intermediate with the same subject DN); (2) Send + Sync of the slow-path future (this is sync code; non-issue but the compile-time assertion is only on Error, not Verifier — PKIX-q9hv.22 already covers); (3) malicious AIA-fetched DER that decodes successfully as a Certificate but carries pathological extensions designed to crash downstream consumers — out of scope for chain-build but worth a separate pkix-path differential fuzz pass.

Would raise confidence if: (a) a test added that submits a leaf with 100 distinct AIA URIs and asserts the fetcher is called at most MAX_URIS_PER_CERT times (would validate PKIX-q9hv.31); (b) a test added that submits a leaf whose AIA URI points at 127.0.0.1 and asserts that the default fetcher refuses (would validate PKIX-q9hv.32 once a SSRF guard ships in pkix-aia-http); (c) read pkix-path-builder source end-to-end for any path that re-canonicalizes Certificate fields, which would close the PKIX-q9hv.4 invariant gap.
Idiom rating (supplement, run-bd-review-rusty-20260514, model: claude-opus-4-7, /review-rusty pass 2): ACCEPTABLE — confirms prior pass's verdict. Read the 7 new test files (~2000 LoC) the prior pass admitted not reading in depth; filed one new finding (PKIX-q9hv.34, P2 chore) for byte-identical load_fixture + NOW/BEFORE/anchors duplication across 8 disk-reading test files. No unsafe blocks anywhere in the diff (confirmed via grep across pkix-chain/src and pkix-chain/tests). No new design-level idiom issues. Production code is straightforward Rust that a serious Rust practitioner would nod at — the trait-bounded Verifier with default-NoAiaFetcher generic, the From-impl coverage on Error, the static-promotion trick at line 444 with the explanatory comment, the #[forbid(unsafe_code)] crate header, and the Send+Sync compile-time assertion are all idiomatic. The mechanical clippy-tier issues (PKIX-q9hv.26 / .27 / .28 / .30 / .34) are all bounded; none touch the design seam.
Rust idiom confidence (supplement, run-bd-review-rusty-20260514, model: claude-opus-4-7): ~90% chance of missed issue. Slightly above prior pass's 85% because I read the 7 new test files end-to-end (1972 LoC across hostname_corpus, mailbox_corpus, verify_tls_server, verify_tls_client, verify_smime, verify_code_signer, verify_time_stamper, verify_ocsp_responder, serde_round_trip, aia_chain_build, aia_http_e2e) that the prior pass admitted skipping. Least confident flag: PKIX-q9hv.34 itself is on the boundary between 'real DRY finding' (8 byte-identical fn load_fixture copies, verified via md5sum) and 'pre-1.0 introduces-a-new-workspace-convention' — no tests/common/mod.rs exists anywhere in the workspace today, so adopting it for pkix-chain is a new pattern, not an existing one. A reasonable maintainer could close as wontfix on the grounds that duplication is bounded and the cost of introducing a cross-test module is non-zero; I stand by the P2 priority because the 8-way byte-identical duplication will recur every time someone changes fixture loading. Uncertainty driven by: (1) review-readonly constraint kept me from running cargo clippy --all-features -p pkix-chain -- -D warnings, which would surface any low-level idiom lints I missed by visual inspection — clippy's pedantic ruleset in particular has wide coverage of the for _iteration / if let chains / .clone() / format!-vs-to_string class of issues; (2) I did not run cargo fmt --check on the diff; (3) I did not re-derive prior findings PKIX-q9hv.26 / .27 / .28 against my fresh read of aia_extract.rs — I noted their applicability and the prior findings cover the same locations, but I did not double-verify each citation; (4) the duplication argument for PKIX-q9hv.34 hinges partly on 'similar test files in pkix-revocation, pkix-truststore, and other crates will copy the same pattern' — I did not actually inspect those crates' test directories to confirm that prediction. Would raise confidence if: (a) cargo clippy --all-features -p pkix-chain -- -D warnings runs cleanly (would confirm no clippy lints in the diff), (b) cargo fmt --check passes on the new test files (would confirm no formatting drift, especially around the verify_* wrappers' multi-line argument lists), (c) PKIX-q9hv.34 is reviewed against the workspace's posture on tests/common/mod.rs as a convention — if the maintainer's stance is 'no test-shared-helpers conventions yet, defer until pattern recurs in a second crate', the finding should be deferred rather than implemented.
Crypto-security supplement re-pass (second invocation, run-bd-review-crypto-security-20260514T-2nd, model: claude-opus-4-7, /review-crypto-security).

Re-read pkix-chain/src/lib.rs (1667 LoC) and aia_extract.rs (115 LoC) end-to-end independent of the prior pass. Cross-checked against the prior crypto-security findings (.31, .32, .33) and the security-lens annotations on .3, .4, .12.

Findings filed: 0 new. Confirmed coverage of all skill sections (A–G):
- A (key material): N/A — pkix-chain holds no secret material. Confirmed fixture private keys in gen.py are ephemeral (generated at fixture build time, not committed; only .der certs in tests/fixtures/).
- B (side channels): N/A — every comparison is on public data (DN bytes via names_match, OID equality, serial-number bytes in LeafIdent, EKU/KU bitmasks).
- C (untrusted input at boundaries): Covered by prior pass.
  - aia_extract::ca_issuers_http_uris handles malformed AIA AuthorityInfoAccessSyntax::from_der by returning Vec::new() — total parser, no panic path.
  - `<Certificate as der::Decode>::from_der(&der)` on AIA-fetched bytes is delegated to x509-cert; defense-in-depth size cap covered by PKIX-q9hv.33.
  - is_http_scheme is a length-checked ASCII compare with no panic path.
- D (RNG): N/A — no randomness consumed in pkix-chain production paths.
- E (persistent storage): N/A — pkix-chain has no storage layer.
- F (logging): No log statements anywhere in production code paths. Error::Display interpolates DN-text reasons and underlying error messages, none of which carry secret-class data.
- G (algorithm and parameter choice): Covered. DefaultVerifier wires RSA-PKCS1v15-SHA-{256,384,512}, ECDSA-P-256-SHA-256, optionally ECDSA-P-384-SHA-384. PKCS1v15 in signature-verify direction is sound (Bleichenbacher applies only to RSA encryption). No SHA-1, MD5, DES, RC4. RFC 3161 §2.3 + §2.1 #10 EKU/KU sole-value enforcement (enforce_timestamping_eku_critical_and_sole + enforce_timestamping_ku_shape) is spec-correct.

Candidate findings considered and dropped:
1. NoCheckShim leaf-identity check fires on any cert in chain matching (issuer-DN, serial) — dropped, already captured by PKIX-q9hv.4 (LeafIdent byte-equality) which has the security lens applied.
2. has_ocsp_no_check read BEFORE verify_chain validates the chain — dropped, no exploit path because verify_chain still must validate the responder's signature; nocheck bypass only affects revocation, and a forged responder cert cannot validate against the issuer's SPKI.
3. Slow-path AIA fetch on a wrong-ordered chain (caller submits [intermediate, leaf, root] with chain[0]=intermediate) — dropped, this is API-contract caller-side mistake, not a workspace defect.
4. is_aia_recoverable includes SignatureInvalid but pool.add doesn't remove the wrong-key cert — dropped, this is captured by PKIX-q9hv.2 as a correctness/availability bug. The trust-model analysis: an attacker who injects a wrong-key intermediate into the supplied chain cannot upgrade it via AIA because the wrong-key cert cannot validate against any leaf; the path-builder either fails or succeeds with the correct intermediate fetched alongside. No security regression.
5. AIA-fetched cert decoded successfully but is unrelated to the chain — dropped, the path-builder's path enumeration enforces DN linkage and signature verification on every candidate path; an unrelated cert in the pool is harmless because it cannot form a valid path.
6. Send + Sync on Verifier itself — dropped, this is API-contract / idiom concern captured by PKIX-q9hv.22. Not security-class. The Send+Sync compile-time assertion at lib.rs:1538-1541 covers Error specifically.
7. aia_extract::ca_issuers_http_uris has no per-cert URI count cap inside the helper — dropped, captured by PKIX-q9hv.31 (fan-out cap at the build_with_aia caller level is the appropriate place).

Time spent on this re-pass: ~35 minutes. Read both production source files (1782 LoC) in full. Did not re-read the 7 new test files (the prior /review-rusty supplement on this epic already read them; no security-relevant test gap surfaced from spot-checks of file listings).

Probability a competent third-party crypto reviewer would find a P0 I did not flag: ~5–10%, unchanged from the prior pass's ~10%. The same uncertainties apply: (a) interaction of AIA-augmented pool with pkix-path-builder's DFS on cross-signed certs (covered by PKIX-q9hv.1 / .2 / .4 as correctness items), (b) the LeafIdent byte-equality assumption (captured at .4), (c) pkix-aia-http SSRF guards out of scope for this epic (the trust-model gap in pkix-chain itself is captured at .32).

No primary review epic actions taken. Per the skill's CLOSING section, $EPIC ownership stays with the primary review.
